      <title>kagent v1.0 Can Run Claude Code as a Managed Kubernetes Agent</title>
      <dc:creator>Mike Moore</dc:creator>
      <pubDate>Fri, 18 Sep 2026 16:10:21 +0000</pubDate>
      <link>https://dev.to/webofmike/kagent-v10-can-run-claude-code-as-a-managed-kubernetes-agent-3p50</link>
      <guid>https://dev.to/webofmike/kagent-v10-can-run-claude-code-as-a-managed-kubernetes-agent-3p50</guid>
      <description><p><em>Originally published at <a href="https://webofmike.com/kagent-v1-agentinstance-claude-code-harness/?utm_source=devto&amp;utm_medium=syndication&amp;utm_campaign=kagent-v1-agentinstance-claude-code-harness" rel="noopener noreferrer">webofmike.com</a> on 2026-09-18. The demo repo and every command in it were run before publishing.</em></p>

<p>kagent shipped <a href="https://github.com/kagent-dev/kagent/releases/tag/v1.0.0-alpha1" rel="noopener noreferrer">v1.0.0-alpha1</a> this morning, its first 1.0 line after nine months on 0.x. The tag says alpha; GitHub's own release flag says otherwise; it's marked <code>prerelease: false</code>, listed as <code>Latest</code>. Release notes lie about formatting more than they should, and this is a version-number one: don't assume the tag string tells you how GitHub, or a Helm repo index, actually classifies the artifact. Check both, every time.</p>

<p>The changelog runs to roughly 130 pull requests. Most of it is refactoring: <code>refactor: remove deployment-backed agent API</code>, <code>refactor: remove legacy controller runtime</code>, <code>chore: remove legacy ACP and controller runtime</code>. That pattern, repeated a dozen times, is the actual story. kagent didn't add a feature to its old agent model. It replaced the model.</p>

<h2>
  
  
  AgentInstance replaces the Deployment
</h2>

<p>Through 0.x, a kagent agent was, underneath, a Kubernetes Deployment. v1.0 introduces <code>AgentInstance</code>: an imperative gRPC lifecycle object with a fixed state machine, not a workload spec a controller reconciles toward.</p>

<p><a href="https://github.com/kagent-dev/kagent/pull/2436" rel="noopener noreferrer">PR #2436</a> adds the service and its PostgreSQL persistence, with idempotent create, ownership checks, and Actor identity fencing. <a href="https://github.com/kagent-dev/kagent/pull/2445" rel="noopener noreferrer">PR #2445</a> adds suspend and resume, synchronous, backed by Substrate, and explicit about what happens when two callers collide:</p>

<blockquote>
<p>Kind smoke: Create → READY → Suspend → SUSPENDED → Resume → READY → conflicting Resume → ABORTED → Delete → DELETED → Get → NOT_FOUND</p>
</blockquote>

<p>That's not a happy-path test. It's a test that a second, conflicting resume gets rejected outright rather than racing the first one. A Deployment reconciler doesn't offer that; it just converges, eventually, and two competing writers get whatever order the informer delivers. AgentInstance answers with a status code instead.</p>

<p><a href="https://github.com/kagent-dev/kagent/pull/2446" rel="noopener noreferrer">PR #2446</a> puts an authenticated A2A gRPC gateway in front of ready instances, routing through Atenet to private root Substrate actors. The PR is explicit about what's still missing: "Durable public Task persistence, public/private ID mapping, ordering, and idempotency remain follow-up work." Worth knowing before you point production A2A traffic at it on day one of an alpha.</p>

<h2>
  
  
  Checkpoint and fork, at the conversation level
</h2>

<p>The most visible v1.0 feature lives in the chat UI, not the API. <a href="https://github.com/kagent-dev/kagent/pull/2775" rel="noopener noreferrer">PR #2775</a> adds a Checkpoint button next to Send. It saves the conversation's current turn boundary. "Everything above it travels into a fork and nothing below it does" is how the PR describes the contract. <code>Duplicate chat</code> in the rail's row menu is the same mechanism: checkpoint plus fork, in one click.</p>

<p><a href="https://github.com/kagent-dev/kagent/pull/2847" rel="noopener noreferrer">PR #2847</a> renames the concept from "checkpoint" to "snapshot" in the chat, gives each one a name (<code>&lt;agentInstanceId&gt;-&lt;headTaskId&gt;</code> by default), and puts Fork, Rename, and Delete on its mark in the transcript. <a href="https://github.com/kagent-dev/kagent/pull/2804" rel="noopener noreferrer">PR #2804</a> adds deletion: releasing a checkpoint's snapshot doesn't break chats already forked from it, because a fork copies the checkpoint's identity rather than referencing it live.</p>

<p>This is a git-like model applied to an agent conversation, and it's a genuinely different way to think about agent state. An agent conversation that goes sideways isn't something you restart from scratch or patch in place; you fork from the last good checkpoint and try again, keeping the bad branch around to compare.</p>

<h2>
  
  
  Golden snapshots: resuming without a cold OCI boot
</h2>

<p>The performance story sits underneath the UI, in <a href="https://github.com/kagent-dev/kagent/pull/2715" rel="noopener noreferrer">PR #2715</a>: resuming a suspended actor from a Substrate "golden snapshot" (a FULL gVisor snapshot plus the latest DATA snapshot) instead of cold-booting the actor from its OCI image every time.</p>

<p>The PR includes its own benchmark, 25 turns per harness, cold boot versus golden resume:</p>

<div class="table-wrapper-paragraph"><table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Metric</th>
<th>Codex: cold / golden</th>
<th>Claude: cold / golden</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Median first output</td>
<td>725 / 695 ms</td>
<td>1,282 / 1,068 ms</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Median turn completion</td>
<td>971 / 957 ms</td>
<td>2,007 / 1,731 ms</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Mean Substrate restore</td>
<td>235 / 234 ms</td>
<td>294 / 196 ms</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Mean checkpoint</td>
<td>232 / 232 ms</td>
<td>243 / 212 ms</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table></div>

<p>Codex barely moves. Claude's numbers move more, which tracks: a heavier CLI process pays more for a cold OCI boot and gets more back from skipping it. I haven't reproduced this benchmark myself; it's quoted from the PR description, not a run against my own cluster, and I'm saying so rather than presenting it as something I measured.</p>

<p>The PR is also specific about when an old golden snapshot stops working: a Substrate upgrade doesn't automatically invalidate one, because the snapshot manifest pins its own sandbox class, runtime asset hash, and pause image. It breaks only if an upgrade changes the snapshot format itself, or the restore contract, or drops host support for the pinned runtime. That's a real answer to "what happens to my snapshots when I upgrade Substrate," not a "should be fine" hand-wave.</p>

<h2>
  
  
  The new harnesses: Claude Code and Codex, running as agents
</h2>

<p>The change I'd call the headline feature is <a href="https://github.com/kagent-dev/kagent/pull/2602" rel="noopener noreferrer">PR #2602</a>: kagent can now run the actual Claude Code CLI as an agent harness, pinned version, over A2A, with streaming, cancellation, session resume, and durable state through Substrate. <a href="https://github.com/kagent-dev/kagent/pull/2645" rel="noopener noreferrer">PR #2645</a> adds Codex the same way, reusing most of the Claude harness's plumbing, driven through the Codex App Server's JSON-RPC-over-stdio protocol.</p>

<p>That means kagent's own harness options are no longer limited to its ADK-based agent runtime. You can point an <code>AgentTemplate</code> at a coding CLI you already use daily and get a managed, checkpointable, forkable, suspend-and-resume-capable Kubernetes object wrapped around it.</p>

<p>One detail in the Codex PR is worth calling out on its own, because it looks alarming out of context and isn't:</p>

<blockquote>
<p>Runs Codex with approvals set to never and native sandboxing set to danger-full-access; the Substrate Actor is intentionally the security boundary.</p>
</blockquote>

<p>Read on its own, "danger-full-access" sounds like turning off the safety rails. It's the opposite: kagent is deliberately not layering Codex's own approval prompts and sandbox on top of Substrate's, because that would be two enforcement points guessing about each other's state. The Substrate actor, the gVisor sandbox the harness runs inside, is the one boundary that's actually authoritative, so the harness-level controls are turned off rather than left to fight it. Whether you're comfortable with that tradeoff depends entirely on trusting the actor sandbox, which is a fair thing to want to verify yourself before running either harness against anything sensitive.</p>

<h2>
  
  
  What v1.0.0-alpha1 doesn't mean
</h2>

<p>Alpha means alpha. The A2A gateway PR names its own gaps in durable task persistence and ID mapping. This release also carries <code>fix: migrate checkpoints to Substrate v0.0.26</code> and <code>fix: preserve conversation identity and history across forks</code> as <em>fixes</em>, both landing after the checkpoint/fork UI they support, which says the fork feature had real correctness bugs during its own development window. That's normal for a feature this new, not a red flag, but it means an alpha this size is worth running somewhere you can afford to lose state before you run it somewhere you can't.</p>

<p>The architecture change is bigger than any one feature in it. kagent spent most of 2026 running agents as pods that Agent Substrate multiplexed onto a shared worker pool (<a href="https://webofmike.com/kagent-agent-substrate/" rel="noopener noreferrer">I wrote about that runtime here</a>). v1.0 keeps that runtime and puts a proper lifecycle API on top of it: agents you can suspend, resume, checkpoint, and fork as first-class operations, not side effects of a Deployment you're poking with kubectl. Adding Claude Code and Codex as harnesses on that same lifecycle is what makes it concrete: whatever you build against AgentInstance now works for a coding agent you already trust, not just kagent's own runtime.</p>

<p>Full changelog: <a href="https://github.com/kagent-dev/kagent/releases/tag/v1.0.0-alpha1" rel="noopener noreferrer">kagent-dev/kagent v1.0.0-alpha1</a>. Compare against the last stable line: <a href="https://github.com/kagent-dev/kagent/compare/v0.10.0-rc1...v1.0.0-alpha1" rel="noopener noreferrer">v0.10.0...v1.0.0-alpha1</a>.</p>

<h2>
  
  
  Frequently asked questions
</h2>

<p><strong>Can I run Claude Code as an agent inside kagent on Kubernetes?</strong></p>

<p>Yes, as of kagent v1.0.0-alpha1. PR #2602 adds a native Claude harness that runs the pinned Claude Code CLI over A2A with streaming, cancellation, session resume, and durable state on Substrate. PR #2645 adds the same support for Codex, reusing most of the same plumbing, with feature parity to kagent's own ADK harness.</p>

<p><strong>What is an AgentInstance in kagent v1.0?</strong></p>

<p>AgentInstance is kagent v1.0's replacement for its old Deployment-backed agent API. It is an imperative gRPC lifecycle object, create/suspend/resume/delete, backed by Substrate actors and persisted in PostgreSQL. Competing transitions are conflict-fenced: a second resume against an already-resumed instance returns ABORTED instead of corrupting state.</p>

<p><strong>How much faster is resuming a kagent agent from a golden snapshot than cold-booting it?</strong></p>

<p>In kagent's own PR #2715 benchmark (25 turns per harness), the Claude harness's median turn completion dropped from 2,007ms cold to 1,731ms from a golden snapshot, and mean Substrate restore dropped from 294ms to 196ms. Codex, a lighter process, moved less: 971ms to 957ms median turn completion. Both numbers come from the PR description, not a run I reproduced myself.</p>

<p><strong>Can I fork a kagent conversation without losing earlier checkpoints?</strong></p>

<p>Yes. kagent v1.0's UI lets you checkpoint a chat turn, then fork from that checkpoint into a new, independent conversation that inherits the checkpoint's name (PR #2775, #2847). Deleting a checkpoint later releases the snapshot it pins, but chats already forked from it keep working (PR #2804).</p>

</description>

      <title>Two agentgateway CEL Gotchas: One Fails Open, One Fails Closed</title>
      <dc:creator>Mike Moore</dc:creator>
      <pubDate>Fri, 18 Sep 2026 16:09:49 +0000</pubDate>
      <link>https://dev.to/webofmike/two-agentgateway-cel-gotchas-one-fails-open-one-fails-closed-17eg</link>
      <guid>https://dev.to/webofmike/two-agentgateway-cel-gotchas-one-fails-open-one-fails-closed-17eg</guid>
      <description><p><em>Originally published at <a href="https://webofmike.com/agentgateway-cel-authorization-gotchas/?utm_source=devto&amp;utm_medium=syndication&amp;utm_campaign=agentgateway-cel-authorization-gotchas" rel="noopener noreferrer">webofmike.com</a> on 2026-09-18. The demo repo and every command in it were run before publishing.</em></p>

<p>I was writing a CEL authorization policy for an LLM route in <a href="https://docs.solo.io/agentgateway/" rel="noopener noreferrer">Solo Enterprise for agentgateway</a>: restrict which models a caller may reach, and refuse callers whose identity provider says they are in a jurisdiction the company cannot serve. Two conditions, both read off the same request.</p>

<p>The first version I wrote allowed a request it should have denied. The second version denied every request, including the ones that should have passed. Neither one reported an error. Both showed <code>Accepted</code> and <code>Attached</code> in the policy status.</p>

<p>The working policy and the demo that proves it are in <a href="https://github.com/themsquared/agentic-demo" rel="noopener noreferrer">themsquared/agentic-demo</a> under <a href="https://github.com/themsquared/agentic-demo/tree/main/manifests/governance" rel="noopener noreferrer"><code>manifests/governance/</code></a>. Everything below was verified against a live cluster running v2026.8.2.</p>

<h2>
  
  
  The policy I meant to write
</h2>

<p>Two rules on a route called <code>governed-llm</code>. The caller's JWT carries a <code>country</code> claim from the identity provider. The request body names a model.</p>

<ol>
<li>The country must be present and not on a restricted list.</li>
<li>The model must be one the AI governance group has approved.</li>
</ol>

<p>Written the obvious way, that is two entries in <code>matchExpressions</code>:<br>
</p>

<div class="highlight js-code-highlight">
<pre class="highlight yaml"><code><span class="na">traffic</span><span class="pi">:</span>
  <span class="na">authorization</span><span class="pi">:</span>
    <span class="na">action</span><span class="pi">:</span> <span class="s">Allow</span>
    <span class="na">policy</span><span class="pi">:</span>
      <span class="na">matchExpressions</span><span class="pi">:</span>
      <span class="pi">-</span> <span class="s2">"</span><span class="s">has(jwt.country)</span><span class="nv"> </span><span class="s">&amp;&amp;</span><span class="nv"> </span><span class="s">!(jwt.country</span><span class="nv"> </span><span class="s">in</span><span class="nv"> </span><span class="s">['CU',</span><span class="nv"> </span><span class="s">'IR',</span><span class="nv"> </span><span class="s">'KP',</span><span class="nv"> </span><span class="s">'SY'])"</span>
      <span class="pi">-</span> <span class="s2">"</span><span class="s">json(request.body).model</span><span class="nv"> </span><span class="s">in</span><span class="nv"> </span><span class="s">['claude-sonnet-4-6',</span><span class="nv"> </span><span class="s">'claude-haiku-4-5']"</span>
</code></pre>

</div>



<p>That reads as "both must hold". It is not what it does.</p>

<h2>
  
  
  Failure one: matchExpressions is OR, and it fails open
</h2>

<p>I have two test users from the same Keycloak realm, in the same group, with the same permissions. The only difference is the <code>country</code> claim: <code>maria</code> is <code>US</code>, <code>pat</code> is <code>IR</code>.</p>

<p>With the two-entry policy above:</p>

<div class="table-wrapper-paragraph"><table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Caller</th>
<th>Model</th>
<th>Expected</th>
<th>Actual</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>maria (US)</td>
<td>approved</td>
<td>200</td>
<td>200</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>pat (IR)</td>
<td>approved</td>
<td><strong>403</strong></td>
<td><strong>200</strong></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>maria (US)</td>
<td>not approved</td>
<td><strong>403</strong></td>
<td><strong>200</strong></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>no JWT</td>
<td>approved</td>
<td>401</td>
<td>401</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table></div>

<p>Both of the requests that should have been refused went through to the provider.</p>

<p>The reason is that entries in <code>matchExpressions</code> are OR'ed. A request is allowed when <em>any</em> expression evaluates true. <code>pat</code> fails the country rule but satisfies the model rule, so the policy allows the request. <code>maria</code> asking for an unapproved model is the mirror image: the country rule passes, so the model rule never gets to matter.</p>

<p>The <a href="https://docs.solo.io/agentgateway/" rel="noopener noreferrer">documentation</a> does state the behavior, in one sentence: requests that do not match any of the conditions are denied. Read closely that is unambiguous. Read at the speed you actually read reference docs, next to a YAML block with a list under it, and "a list of conditions" looks like a list of requirements.</p>

<p>The fix is to stop treating the list as a conjunction and write one expression:<br>
</p>

<div class="highlight js-code-highlight">
<pre class="highlight yaml"><code><span class="na">matchExpressions</span><span class="pi">:</span>
<span class="pi">-</span> <span class="pi">&gt;-</span>
  <span class="s">has(jwt.country) &amp;&amp; !(jwt.country in ['CU', 'IR', 'KP', 'SY'])</span>
  <span class="s">&amp;&amp; json(request.body).model in ['claude-sonnet-4-6', 'claude-haiku-4-5']</span>
</code></pre>

</div>



<p>Same two conditions, one entry, joined with <code>&amp;&amp;</code>. Now the table comes out right:</p>

<div class="table-wrapper-paragraph"><table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Caller</th>
<th>Model</th>
<th>Result</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>maria (US)</td>
<td>approved</td>
<td>200</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>pat (IR)</td>
<td>approved</td>
<td><strong>403</strong></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>maria (US)</td>
<td>not approved</td>
<td><strong>403</strong></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>no JWT</td>
<td>approved</td>
<td>401</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table></div>

<p>What makes this one worth writing down is the direction of the failure. A policy with one entry per rule is the natural way to write it, it looks correct in review, the resource reports healthy, and it permits traffic. Nothing surfaces until someone audits denials that never happened.</p>

<p>If your allowlist is per-credential rather than per-claim, there is a second place to put it: agentgateway v1.5.0 added an <code>allowedModels</code> list directly on the API key, which I covered in <a href="https://webofmike.com/agentgateway-per-key-llm-budgets/" rel="noopener noreferrer">per-key LLM budgets that return 429</a>. The CEL route is the one to use when the decision depends on something in the token rather than on which key was presented.</p>

<h2>
  
  
  Failure two: llm.requestModel is empty when authorization runs
</h2>

<p>Fixing the first bug, I reached for what looked like the correct variable. agentgateway exposes an <code>llm</code> context with the model, the provider, token counts, and realized cost. Reading the model from there is cleaner than parsing the body:<br>
</p>

<div class="highlight js-code-highlight">
<pre class="highlight yaml"><code><span class="na">matchExpressions</span><span class="pi">:</span>
<span class="pi">-</span> <span class="s2">"</span><span class="s">llm.requestModel</span><span class="nv"> </span><span class="s">in</span><span class="nv"> </span><span class="s">['claude-sonnet-4-6',</span><span class="nv"> </span><span class="s">'claude-haiku-4-5']"</span>
</code></pre>

</div>



<p>Every request now returned 403. Not just the ones naming an unapproved model. All of them, including a request for a model literally present in that list.</p>

<p><code>llm.requestModel</code> exists, and it is documented. It belongs to the backend AI phase, which runs after routing has selected a backend. A <code>traffic.authorization</code> policy runs earlier, at the route level. At that point the <code>llm</code> context has not been populated, the expression cannot evaluate true, and a policy whose action is <code>Allow</code> denies everything.</p>

<p>This one fails closed, which is the safer direction, but it is confusing in a specific way: the policy looks like it is working. Requests for unapproved models get 403, exactly as designed. You only catch it if your test set includes a request that is supposed to succeed.</p>

<h2>
  
  
  Isolating which variables actually resolve
</h2>

<p>When a CEL expression silently never matches, the fastest way to find out why is to hold the request constant and vary only the expression. I patched one field on the live policy and re-ran the same two requests each time, one naming an approved model and one naming an unapproved model:<br>
</p>

<div class="highlight js-code-highlight">
<pre class="highlight shell"><code>kubectl patch eagpol cel-probe <span class="nt">-n</span> agentgateway-system <span class="nt">--type</span><span class="o">=</span>json <span class="se">\</span>
  <span class="nt">-p</span> <span class="s2">"[{</span><span class="se">\"</span><span class="s2">op</span><span class="se">\"</span><span class="s2">:</span><span class="se">\"</span><span class="s2">replace</span><span class="se">\"</span><span class="s2">,</span><span class="se">\"</span><span class="s2">path</span><span class="se">\"</span><span class="s2">:</span><span class="se">\"</span><span class="s2">/spec/traffic/authorization/policy/matchExpressions</span><span class="se">\"</span><span class="s2">,</span><span class="se">\"</span><span class="s2">value</span><span class="se">\"</span><span class="s2">:[</span><span class="se">\"</span><span class="nv">$EXPR</span><span class="se">\"</span><span class="s2">]}]"</span>
</code></pre>

</div>



<div class="table-wrapper-paragraph"><table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Expression under test</th>
<th>approved model</th>
<th>unapproved model</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><code>true</code></td>
<td>200</td>
<td>200</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>'admins' in jwt.Groups</code></td>
<td>200</td>
<td>200</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>jwt.preferred_username == 'demo'</code></td>
<td>200</td>
<td>200</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>has(llm.requestModel)</code></td>
<td><strong>403</strong></td>
<td><strong>403</strong></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>llm.requestModel in [...]</code></td>
<td><strong>403</strong></td>
<td><strong>403</strong></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>json(request.body).model in [...]</code></td>
<td>200</td>
<td><strong>403</strong></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table></div>

<p>The first three lines prove the policy is attached and that JWT claims resolve fine at this phase. Line four is the diagnosis: <code>has(llm.requestModel)</code> is false, so the variable is not merely holding an unexpected value, it is absent. The last line is the working form.</p>

<p><code>has()</code> is the probe worth remembering. It separates "this variable holds something I did not expect" from "this variable does not exist here", and those have completely different fixes.</p>

<h2>
  
  
  The policy that works
</h2>

<p>Both findings in one resource:<br>
</p>

<div class="highlight js-code-highlight">
<pre class="highlight yaml"><code><span class="na">apiVersion</span><span class="pi">:</span> <span class="s">enterpriseagentgateway.solo.io/v1alpha1</span>
<span class="na">kind</span><span class="pi">:</span> <span class="s">EnterpriseAgentgatewayPolicy</span>
<span class="na">metadata</span><span class="pi">:</span>
  <span class="na">name</span><span class="pi">:</span> <span class="s">governed-llm-access</span>
  <span class="na">namespace</span><span class="pi">:</span> <span class="s">agentgateway-system</span>
<span class="na">spec</span><span class="pi">:</span>
  <span class="na">targetRefs</span><span class="pi">:</span>
  <span class="pi">-</span> <span class="na">group</span><span class="pi">:</span> <span class="s">gateway.networking.k8s.io</span>
    <span class="na">kind</span><span class="pi">:</span> <span class="s">HTTPRoute</span>
    <span class="na">name</span><span class="pi">:</span> <span class="s">governed-llm</span>
  <span class="na">traffic</span><span class="pi">:</span>
    <span class="na">authorization</span><span class="pi">:</span>
      <span class="na">action</span><span class="pi">:</span> <span class="s">Allow</span>
      <span class="na">policy</span><span class="pi">:</span>
        <span class="na">matchExpressions</span><span class="pi">:</span>
        <span class="pi">-</span> <span class="pi">&gt;-</span>
          <span class="s">has(jwt.country) &amp;&amp; !(jwt.country in ['CU', 'IR', 'KP', 'SY'])</span>
          <span class="s">&amp;&amp; json(request.body).model in ['claude-sonnet-4-6', 'claude-haiku-4-5', 'acme-standard', 'acme-premium']</span>
</code></pre>

</div>



<p><code>acme-standard</code> and <code>acme-premium</code> are virtual model names, mapped to real models by a separate <code>modelAliases</code> policy on the backend. Callers ask for a tier, the platform team decides what that tier means today, and the allowlist keeps naming the same two strings when the underlying model changes.</p>

<p>A denied request gets HTTP 403 with the body <code>authorization failed</code>, and the caller never reaches the provider. That is the part that matters for a jurisdiction rule: nothing was sent upstream, so there is nothing exported, nothing logged on the provider side, and nothing billed.</p>

<h2>
  
  
  Why these two belong in the same post
</h2>

<p>They are the same class of bug seen from both sides. In each case the policy compiles, the controller reports it healthy, and the resource status says <code>Accepted</code> and <code>Attached</code>. The only signal is the HTTP status of a request you have to think to send.</p>

<p>That suggests a test set rather than a review habit. For any allow-style authorization policy, send four requests: one that should pass, one that fails each condition independently, and one with no credential at all. The OR bug is invisible unless you send a request that violates exactly one condition. The phase bug is invisible unless you send one that violates none.<br>
</p>

<div class="highlight js-code-highlight">
<pre class="highlight shell"><code><span class="c"># should pass</span>
curl <span class="nt">-s</span> <span class="nt">-o</span> /dev/null <span class="nt">-w</span> <span class="s1">'%{http_code}\n'</span> localhost:8081/governed-llm/v1/chat/completions <span class="se">\</span>
  <span class="nt">-H</span> <span class="s2">"Authorization: Bearer </span><span class="nv">$MARIA</span><span class="s2">"</span> <span class="nt">-H</span> <span class="s1">'content-type: application/json'</span> <span class="se">\</span>
  <span class="nt">-d</span> <span class="s1">'{"model":"acme-standard","max_tokens":8,"messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Say OK."}]}'</span>

<span class="c"># violates the country rule only</span>
curl <span class="nt">-s</span> <span class="nt">-o</span> /dev/null <span class="nt">-w</span> <span class="s1">'%{http_code}\n'</span> localhost:8081/governed-llm/v1/chat/completions <span class="se">\</span>
  <span class="nt">-H</span> <span class="s2">"Authorization: Bearer </span><span class="nv">$PAT</span><span class="s2">"</span> <span class="nt">-H</span> <span class="s1">'content-type: application/json'</span> <span class="se">\</span>
  <span class="nt">-d</span> <span class="s1">'{"model":"acme-standard","max_tokens":8,"messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Say OK."}]}'</span>

<span class="c"># violates the model rule only</span>
curl <span class="nt">-s</span> <span class="nt">-o</span> /dev/null <span class="nt">-w</span> <span class="s1">'%{http_code}\n'</span> localhost:8081/governed-llm/v1/chat/completions <span class="se">\</span>
  <span class="nt">-H</span> <span class="s2">"Authorization: Bearer </span><span class="nv">$MARIA</span><span class="s2">"</span> <span class="nt">-H</span> <span class="s1">'content-type: application/json'</span> <span class="se">\</span>
  <span class="nt">-d</span> <span class="s1">'{"model":"claude-opus-4-1","max_tokens":8,"messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Say OK."}]}'</span>

<span class="c"># no credential</span>
curl <span class="nt">-s</span> <span class="nt">-o</span> /dev/null <span class="nt">-w</span> <span class="s1">'%{http_code}\n'</span> localhost:8081/governed-llm/v1/chat/completions <span class="se">\</span>
  <span class="nt">-H</span> <span class="s1">'content-type: application/json'</span> <span class="se">\</span>
  <span class="nt">-d</span> <span class="s1">'{"model":"acme-standard","max_tokens":8,"messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Say OK."}]}'</span>
</code></pre>

</div>



<p>Expected: <code>200</code>, <code>403</code>, <code>403</code>, <code>401</code>. Anything else and one of the two bugs above is in your policy.</p>

<h2>
  
  
  Running it
</h2>

<p>The demo lives in <a href="https://github.com/themsquared/agentic-demo" rel="noopener noreferrer">themsquared/agentic-demo</a>. It needs a Solo Enterprise license, since <code>EnterpriseAgentgatewayPolicy</code> is an enterprise CRD.<br>
</p>

<div class="highlight js-code-highlight">
<pre class="highlight shell"><code>./setup.sh              <span class="c"># k3d cluster, mesh, gateway, agents (~15 min)</span>
./port-forward.sh
./governance-demo.sh <span class="nt">--check</span>
</code></pre>

</div>



<p><code>--check</code> runs the whole governance walkthrough non-interactively and asserts 24 outcomes, including the four status codes above. The authorization act is <code>--act 2</code> if you only want that part.</p>

<p>The policy discussed here is <a href="https://github.com/themsquared/agentic-demo/blob/main/manifests/governance/02-ofac-model-allowlist.yaml" rel="noopener noreferrer"><code>02-ofac-model-allowlist.yaml</code></a>, and both gotchas are written into the file's header comment so the next person to edit it does not re-derive them.</p>

<p>Next on this route: the same request body, read by a web application firewall instead of a policy engine, so the prompt itself gets inspected rather than just the claims around it.</p>

<h2>
  
  
  Frequently asked questions
</h2>

<p><strong>Are agentgateway matchExpressions AND'ed or OR'ed together?</strong></p>

<p>They are OR'ed. A request is allowed when any single expression in the list evaluates true, so writing two entries produces a policy that permits a request satisfying either one. To require several conditions at once, join them with &amp;&amp; inside one expression. The failure is silent: both forms report Accepted and Attached in the policy status, and only a request that should have been denied reveals the difference.</p>

<p><strong>Why does my agentgateway CEL policy return 403 for every request?</strong></p>

<p>Most often because the expression references a variable that is not populated in the phase where the policy runs. Under traffic.authorization the llm.* variables are empty, so llm.requestModel resolves to nothing and the expression is never true, denying every request including valid ones. Read the model from json(request.body).model instead, which is available at that phase.</p>

<p><strong>How do I check which LLM model a caller requested in a CEL policy?</strong></p>

<p>At the traffic authorization phase, parse the request body: json(request.body).model. The llm.requestModel variable exists but belongs to the backend AI phase, which runs after routing, so it is unavailable to a route-level authorization policy. Verified on Solo Enterprise for agentgateway v2026.8.2 by testing both forms against the same route.</p>

      <title>The Audit Log Confirmed They Got a Shell. It Didn't Say What They Typed.</title>
      <dc:creator>Rocky</dc:creator>
      <pubDate>Fri, 18 Sep 2026 16:05:26 +0000</pubDate>
      <link>https://dev.to/rockyyy/the-audit-log-confirmed-they-got-a-shell-it-didnt-say-what-they-typed-4o1o</link>
      <guid>https://dev.to/rockyyy/the-audit-log-confirmed-they-got-a-shell-it-didnt-say-what-they-typed-4o1o</guid>
      <description><p>A pod gets flagged mid-incident: unexpected outbound connections, a process nobody recognizes. The responder pulls the Kubernetes audit log to reconstruct what happened, and there it is, right where it should be: a <code>create</code> event against <code>pods/exec</code> on that exact pod, timestamp, source IP, the service account that made the call. Confirmation that someone got a shell into the container. Relief for about ten seconds, until the actual question comes up: what did they do once they were in there. The log has nothing. Not "nothing useful." Nothing at all.</p>

<p>This isn't a misconfiguration and it isn't the responder missing a setting. <code>exec</code> (along with <code>attach</code> and <code>port-forward</code>) isn't a normal REST call the API server handles as a single request and response. It's a streaming connection, upgraded to SPDY or WebSocket, that carries the interactive session, your keystrokes going one way, stdout and stderr coming back the other, for as long as the shell stays open. Kubernetes' audit machinery logs API requests as structured events with an optional request and response body depending on the audit policy's verbosity. But the exec session's actual traffic never travels as a request or response body in the first place, it's a raw bidirectional stream on top of the upgraded connection. Turn your audit policy up to the most verbose level available and you still get the same result: the event that says an exec happened, and silence on what happened inside it.</p>

<p>That gap matters most exactly when you need it least to matter, mid-incident, when "what did they run in there" is the first question anyone asks. If your response runbook says "check the audit log for exec commands," it's testing an assumption that isn't true. The audit log will tell you that access happened and roughly when. It will not tell you whether the attacker read a secret, dumped environment variables, or just checked <code>whoami</code> and left.</p>

<p>Closing that gap takes something layered in before the incident, not during it: a runtime security tool that hooks process execution at the node or kernel level (Falco is the common open-source example, watching syscalls directly rather than relying on the API server's view), or routing interactive access through a bastion or kubectl plugin that logs client-side, since the server side of a raw exec session was never going to log it for you. Neither is something you bolt on while triaging a live compromise.</p>

<p>This is the exact translation the Cloud Detection and Response Book is built around, not just AWS CloudTrail or Azure activity logs but the specific blind spots inside Kubernetes' own audit trail, detection-as-code and Sigma rules built with what the platform actually logs (and doesn't) in mind: <a href="https://resources.codelivly.com/product/cloud-pentesting-l2/" rel="noopener noreferrer">https://resources.codelivly.com/product/cloud-pentesting-l2/</a></p>

</description>

      <title>I Deleted the Same Pod Twice. Only One of Them Remembered.</title>
      <dc:creator>Vivian Chiamaka Okose</dc:creator>
      <pubDate>Fri, 18 Sep 2026 15:17:11 +0000</pubDate>
      <link>https://dev.to/vivian_okose/i-deleted-the-same-pod-twice-only-one-of-them-remembered-2g9g</link>
      <guid>https://dev.to/vivian_okose/i-deleted-the-same-pod-twice-only-one-of-them-remembered-2g9g</guid>
      <description><p>I wrote a value to Redis, deleted its pod, and it was gone. Did the same to a different Redis, deleted the pod, and it was still there. Same command, opposite result, and the difference explains what Kubernetes is actually doing.</p>

<h2>
  
  
  The shift: describe, don't instruct
</h2>

<p>Every tool before this took commands that run once. Kubernetes takes a description of what should be true and keeps reality matching it. You say "I want two API pods," and the control plane makes and keeps that true.</p>

<p>The catch: you cannot fix things by hand. Delete a pod, it comes back, because the description still says two. To change what runs, change the description.</p>

<h2>
  
  
  Self-healing, proven
</h2>

<p><a href="https://media2.dev.to/dynamic/image/width=800%2Cheight=%2Cfit=scale-down%2Cgravity=auto%2Cformat=auto/https%3A%2F%2Fdev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com%2Fuploads%2Farticles%2Ftmficbk0g7pusntsr8fm.png" class="article-body-image-wrapper"><img src="https://media2.dev.to/dynamic/image/width=800%2Cheight=%2Cfit=scale-down%2Cgravity=auto%2Cformat=auto/https%3A%2F%2Fdev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com%2Fuploads%2Farticles%2Ftmficbk0g7pusntsr8fm.png" alt="Self-healing" width="782" height="472"></a><br>
<em>Delete a pod and a replacement is scheduled before the old one finishes terminating.<br>
~12 seconds to serving traffic. Nothing responded to the delete specifically, the control loop just saw 1 where it wanted 2.</em></p>

<h2>
  
  
  The pieces
</h2>

<p>Pods wrap containers and are disposable. Deployments hold the replica count and manage pods.<br>
Services give a stable address in front of changing pods, reached by DNS name (<code>redis</code>, not an IP). Labels and selectors are the glue, a Service fronts "anything labelled <code>app: redis</code>", and a label/selector mismatch is the classic beginner bug.</p>

<h2>
  
  
  Autoscaling
</h2>

<p><a href="https://media2.dev.to/dynamic/image/width=800%2Cheight=%2Cfit=scale-down%2Cgravity=auto%2Cformat=auto/https%3A%2F%2Fdev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com%2Fuploads%2Farticles%2Ft99h20hsnalhs5313oh2.png" class="article-body-image-wrapper"><img src="https://media2.dev.to/dynamic/image/width=800%2Cheight=%2Cfit=scale-down%2Cgravity=auto%2Cformat=auto/https%3A%2F%2Fdev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com%2Fuploads%2Farticles%2Ft99h20hsnalhs5313oh2.png" alt="HPA" width="800" height="400"></a><br>
<em>CPU hit 92% under load, pods went 2 to 4 in seconds. Needs metrics-server, and needs pods to declare CPU requests or there's no baseline to measure.</em></p>

<h2>
  
  
  The two Redis pods
</h2>

<p>The API is stateless, interchangeable, perfect for a Deployment. Redis holds data. A plain Deployment loses it on restart. A StatefulSet gives a stable identity (<code>redis-store-0</code>) and a PersistentVolumeClaim that outlives the pod, so the value survives.</p>

<p><a href="https://media2.dev.to/dynamic/image/width=800%2Cheight=%2Cfit=scale-down%2Cgravity=auto%2Cformat=auto/https%3A%2F%2Fdev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com%2Fuploads%2Farticles%2Fwopwaxvv7yo9u278bj0f.png" class="article-body-image-wrapper"><img src="https://media2.dev.to/dynamic/image/width=800%2Cheight=%2Cfit=scale-down%2Cgravity=auto%2Cformat=auto/https%3A%2F%2Fdev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com%2Fuploads%2Farticles%2Fwopwaxvv7yo9u278bj0f.png" alt="StatefulSet PVC" width="800" height="66"></a></p>

<p>Caveat: real replicated databases in Kubernetes are hard (leader election, failover). Most teams use a managed database.</p>

<h2>
  
  
  Config, updates, isolation
</h2>

<p>ConfigMap injects settings as env vars. Rolling updates replace pods gradually, gated by the readiness probe, so a broken version stops the rollout instead of taking the service down.</p>

<p><a href="https://media2.dev.to/dynamic/image/width=800%2Cheight=%2Cfit=scale-down%2Cgravity=auto%2Cformat=auto/https%3A%2F%2Fdev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com%2Fuploads%2Farticles%2F9hvuqcgxa9s4fzz77zrr.png" class="article-body-image-wrapper"><img src="https://media2.dev.to/dynamic/image/width=800%2Cheight=%2Cfit=scale-down%2Cgravity=auto%2Cformat=auto/https%3A%2F%2Fdev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com%2Fuploads%2Farticles%2F9hvuqcgxa9s4fzz77zrr.png" alt="Rollout" width="800" height="221"></a><br>
<em>Rollback adds a revision rather than deleting history, and history is finite. The manifest in git is the real source of truth.</em></p>

<p>By default every pod can reach every other pod. A NetworkPolicy fixes it:</p>

<p><a href="https://media2.dev.to/dynamic/image/width=800%2Cheight=%2Cfit=scale-down%2Cgravity=auto%2Cformat=auto/https%3A%2F%2Fdev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com%2Fuploads%2Farticles%2Fay10sjc2n5cyww4n0884.png" class="article-body-image-wrapper"><img src="https://media2.dev.to/dynamic/image/width=800%2Cheight=%2Cfit=scale-down%2Cgravity=auto%2Cformat=auto/https%3A%2F%2Fdev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com%2Fuploads%2Farticles%2Fay10sjc2n5cyww4n0884.png" alt="NetworkPolicy" width="797" height="114"></a><br>
<em>Unrelated pod: timed out. API with the allowed label: connects. Same chained isolation as AWS security groups, by labels not IPs. The moment a policy selects a pod it goes deny-by-default, so forgetting to allow needed traffic breaks your own app.</em></p>

<h2>
  
  
  Helm vs Kustomize
</h2>

<p>Helm: templated manifests with variables, versioned releases, one-command rollback, but the files aren't valid YAML alone. Kustomize: plain YAML with per-environment patches, no release history, built into kubectl. Helm for third-party software, Kustomize for your own apps. Many teams use both.</p>

<h2>
  
  
  Debugging
</h2>

<p>STATUS gives the category, <code>describe</code> Events give the cause, logs only help once a container starts.</p>

<p><a href="https://media2.dev.to/dynamic/image/width=800%2Cheight=%2Cfit=scale-down%2Cgravity=auto%2Cformat=auto/https%3A%2F%2Fdev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com%2Fuploads%2Farticles%2Foz4cdjssyj6fq0t4c6en.png" class="article-body-image-wrapper"><img src="https://media2.dev.to/dynamic/image/width=800%2Cheight=%2Cfit=scale-down%2Cgravity=auto%2Cformat=auto/https%3A%2F%2Fdev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com%2Fuploads%2Farticles%2Foz4cdjssyj6fq0t4c6en.png" alt="Debug events" width="800" height="561"></a><br>
<em>A deliberate bad-image break. Events name it in one line. Reading Events first is the habit beginners skip.</em></p>

<h2>
  
  
  The one idea
</h2>

<p>Declare the desired state, a control loop keeps reality matching it. Self-healing, autoscaling, rolling updates, rollback, reboot recovery, all the same loop closing a gap.</p>

<p>Full build: <a href="https://github.com/vivianokose/nexaops-operations-lab/tree/main/10-kubernetes" rel="noopener noreferrer">https://github.com/vivianokose/nexaops-operations-lab/tree/main/10-kubernetes</a></p>

</description>

      <title>The two-pod problem: fixing a race condition with pessimistic locking</title>
      <dc:creator>Tushar Sachdeva</dc:creator>
      <pubDate>Fri, 18 Sep 2026 12:56:26 +0000</pubDate>
      <link>https://dev.to/tushar_sachdeva_12a30ff5e/the-two-pod-problem-fixing-a-race-condition-with-pessimistic-locking-2pb8</link>
      <guid>https://dev.to/tushar_sachdeva_12a30ff5e/the-two-pod-problem-fixing-a-race-condition-with-pessimistic-locking-2pb8</guid>
      <description><p>How a five-minute retry delay in an event-driven pipeline turned into a lesson on transaction boundaries — and a 78% drop in event reprocessing.</p>

<p>Before</p>

<p>pod A<br>
pod B<br>
row 402<br>
Both pods write at once → unique-constraint violation → 5-minute retry.</p>

<p>After</p>

<p>pod A<br>
pod B (waits)<br>
row 402<br>
Row lock serializes access — the second pod waits, then sees it's already claimed.</p>

<p>The setup</p>

<p>At Infosys, I work on an event-driven pipeline that reacts to user actions across services. Because we run multiple pods for resiliency, a Message Relay Service polls an event table every 10 seconds looking for freshly captured events to push onto AWS SQS for downstream consumers. Simple in theory — until you run more than one pod.</p>

<p>Where it broke</p>

<p>Two pods, same 10-second poll window, same unprocessed row. Both pick it up. Both try to mark it "in flight" and update its status. One update lands; the other collides with a unique constraint and throws a SQL exception. The event doesn't just retry immediately — it falls into a five-minute backoff, because that window was tuned for a completely different failure mode: transient network errors calling a downstream API. A benign race condition was paying the same tax as a real outage.</p>

<p>Multiply that by the volume of events flowing through the table, and a meaningful slice of "processed" events were either being processed twice or sitting in an unnecessary five-minute queue.</p>

<p>Why the obvious fix doesn't work</p>

<p>The instinctive first move is an application-level check: read the status, see it's UNPROCESSED, then update it. But between the read and the write there's a window — and in a system with more than one pod, something else can slip into that window. It's a textbook time-of-check-to-time-of-use gap, and no amount of if statements inside a single JVM closes it, because the race isn't inside one JVM. It's across two.</p>

<p>What actually closed the gap</p>

<p>The fix wasn't cleverer application code — it was moving the guarantee down to the row itself, with a pessimistic lock:</p>

<p>EventRepository.java</p>

<p>public interface EventRepository extends JpaRepository {</p>

<div class="highlight js-code-highlight">
<pre class="highlight plaintext"><code>@Lock(LockModeType.PESSIMISTIC_WRITE)
@Query("select e from EventEntity e where e.id = :id")
Optional&lt;EventEntity&gt; findForProcessing(@Param("id") Long id);
</code></pre>

</div>

<p>}<br>
EventProcessingService.java</p>

<p>@Transactional<br>
public void processEvent(Long eventId) {<br>
    EventEntity event = eventRepository.findForProcessing(eventId)<br>
        .orElseThrow();</p>

<div class="highlight js-code-highlight">
<pre class="highlight plaintext"><code>if (event.getStatus() != EventStatus.UNPROCESSED) {
    return; // another pod already claimed it
}

event.setStatus(EventStatus.PROCESSING);
eventRepository.save(event);

publishToQueue(event);

event.setStatus(EventStatus.PROCESSED);
eventRepository.save(event);
</code></pre>

</div>

<p>}<br>
PESSIMISTIC_WRITE translates to a SELECT ... FOR UPDATE under the hood. Whichever pod's transaction gets there first holds the row lock until it commits or rolls back; the second pod's transaction simply waits — and when it finally gets the row, it sees the status has already moved to PROCESSING and quietly backs off instead of colliding with a constraint violation.</p>

<p>The lock scope matters here: it's held only for the width of that one row's processing logic, not for the whole batch, so throughput on unrelated rows is untouched.</p>

<p>What changed</p>

<p>Event reprocessing dropped 78% — most of it was this exact race, not real downstream failures.<br>
The five-minute retry delay disappeared for this class of event entirely, since there was no longer an exception to trigger it.<br>
On-call noise dropped too — fewer "why did this event process twice" questions to chase down.<br>
When I'd reach for this again</p>

<p>Pessimistic locking isn't free — a held row lock is a held row lock, and under high contention it can turn into a queue of waiting transactions. It earns its place when contention is rare but the cost of a collision is real (duplicate side effects, constraint violations, silent data drift), and when the locked section stays small. If contention is frequent and collisions are cheap to detect and retry, optimistic locking with a version column is usually the better trade. Here, with a handful of pods racing over the same few rows for a few hundred milliseconds at a time, pessimistic locking was the simpler, more predictable fix.</p>

</description>

      <title>What it takes to trust an open-source app that updates itself</title>
      <dc:creator>UDAWPK</dc:creator>
      <pubDate>Fri, 18 Sep 2026 11:59:27 +0000</pubDate>
      <link>https://dev.to/udawpk_ed5db9215291bfd07d/what-it-takes-to-trust-an-open-source-app-that-updates-itself-3i7e</link>
      <guid>https://dev.to/udawpk_ed5db9215291bfd07d/what-it-takes-to-trust-an-open-source-app-that-updates-itself-3i7e</guid>
      <description><p>An auto-updater is a strange thing to ship in open source. You're asking someone who chose your project specifically because they could read the code to now trust a binary that lands on their machine without them clicking anything.</p>

<p>ROZOOM's <a href="https://github.com/ceh13-community/rozoom/releases/tag/app-v0.23.0" rel="noopener noreferrer">0.23.0 release</a> ships the first version of that channel: a background check, a silent download, and one entry in the notification bell - no toast, no modal stealing focus - "Rozoom 0.23.1 is ready / Restart to finish updating," with a single action, "Restart now." Nothing else changes until you click it.</p>

<p>Here's what that channel actually is, and what happened before we trusted it enough to ship it.</p>

<h2>
  
  
  What actually updates itself
</h2>

<p>The updater works on AppImage (Linux), Windows, and macOS (Apple Silicon) builds. Deb and rpm packages don't auto-update - that's not a footnote, it's the whole story if you're on one of those: you keep updating by hand, the way you already do.</p>

<p>If you're on 0.22.6, this update won't find you automatically. 0.22.6 doesn't have an updater in it at all - there was nothing there to check with. Install 0.23.0 by hand, once. From there, supported platforms take over.</p>

<h2>
  
  
  The part that isn't in the release notes
</h2>

<p>Every update ROZOOM downloads gets checked against a signing key before it's allowed to install. Get that key wrong once and you've built a supply chain for anyone who compromises it.</p>

<p>Ours almost was. The key pair got sent through a messenger app before it ever shipped - a private key and its password, together, outside the places we'd normally trust either. No release had used it yet, so we didn't debate it: we rotated the pair and treated the old one as burned. The cost of doing that before publishing is one line in a config file. After publishing, it's every installed copy losing its update channel for good.</p>

<p>The second thing was less dramatic and more revealing. Turning on this feature meant making the AppImage build a hard requirement instead of a "best effort" step - and the moment we did, it stopped passing. It turned out our AppImage build had been silently failing behind a <code>continue-on-error</code> flag since 0.22.3. Every Linux release for months had shipped without one, and CI stayed green the whole time.</p>

<p>Fixing it for real took three passes, each one a public PR:</p>

<ul>
<li>the build was resolving system libraries from vendored dependency folders instead of the host, and fell over (<a href="https://github.com/ceh13-community/rozoom/pull/160" rel="noopener noreferrer">#160</a>)</li>
<li>that fix exposed a second one: a GTK plugin inheriting the same lookup path and grabbing an incompatible zlib (<a href="https://github.com/ceh13-community/rozoom/pull/161" rel="noopener noreferrer">#161</a>)</li>
<li>only after both landed did a full run go green on Linux, Windows, and macOS together (<a href="https://github.com/ceh13-community/rozoom/pull/159" rel="noopener noreferrer">#159</a>)</li>
</ul>

<h2>
  
  
  What we watched happen
</h2>

<p>0.23.1 existed for exactly one reason: prove the update path works outside CI, on a real machine, not just that the artifacts exist. We installed 0.23.0 fresh, let the updater find 0.23.1 on its own, and let it run start to finish - background check, silent download, one entry in the bell.</p>

<p><a href="https://media2.dev.to/dynamic/image/width=800%2Cheight=%2Cfit=scale-down%2Cgravity=auto%2Cformat=auto/https%3A%2F%2Fdev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com%2Fuploads%2Farticles%2F5lzw89y85vnem9a5r31h.jpeg" class="article-body-image-wrapper"><img src="https://media2.dev.to/dynamic/image/width=800%2Cheight=%2Cfit=scale-down%2Cgravity=auto%2Cformat=auto/https%3A%2F%2Fdev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com%2Fuploads%2Farticles%2F5lzw89y85vnem9a5r31h.jpeg" alt=" " width="800" height="600"></a></p>

<p>Clicked "Restart now," confirmed the one prompt it puts up - any open exec sessions close - and the app came back. Sidebar showed 0.23.1, notification gone, binary hash matching the published release asset.</p>

<p><a href="https://media2.dev.to/dynamic/image/width=800%2Cheight=%2Cfit=scale-down%2Cgravity=auto%2Cformat=auto/https%3A%2F%2Fdev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com%2Fuploads%2Farticles%2Fz2hnya0882a6q2z814n5.jpeg" class="article-body-image-wrapper"><img src="https://media2.dev.to/dynamic/image/width=800%2Cheight=%2Cfit=scale-down%2Cgravity=auto%2Cformat=auto/https%3A%2F%2Fdev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com%2Fuploads%2Farticles%2Fz2hnya0882a6q2z814n5.jpeg" alt=" " width="800" height="600"></a></p>

<h2>
  
  
  Open source
</h2>

<p>ROZOOM is Apache 2.0: <a href="https://github.com/ceh13-community/rozoom" rel="noopener noreferrer">github.com/ceh13-community/rozoom</a>.</p>

<p><a href="https://rozoom.app" rel="noopener noreferrer">https://rozoom.app</a></p>

      <title>Our pods slept for sixty milliseconds out of every hundred</title>
      <dc:creator>Sergey Shinder</dc:creator>
      <pubDate>Fri, 18 Sep 2026 10:22:22 +0000</pubDate>
      <link>https://dev.to/sergey_shinder_ab2d943365/our-pods-slept-for-sixty-milliseconds-out-of-every-hundred-17i5</link>
      <guid>https://dev.to/sergey_shinder_ab2d943365/our-pods-slept-for-sixty-milliseconds-out-of-every-hundred-17i5</guid>
      <description><p>Checkout latency at the ninety ninth percentile sat around nine hundred milliseconds, and the CPU graph for those pods never went above forty percent. We spent a fortnight on the wrong problem because of that graph. Slow code on idle hardware sends you looking at locks, at the database, at anything except the machine that is clearly not busy.</p>

<p>A CPU limit in Kubernetes is not a speed limit in any sense that matches the word. It is a quota per accounting period. Our limit of five hundred millicores meant fifty milliseconds of CPU time in every hundred millisecond window. The service is written in Go, and the runtime sized its parallelism from the node, which has sixty four cores, so it happily ran a dozen goroutines at once. Twelve threads spending fifty milliseconds of quota between them exhaust it in about four milliseconds of wall clock. For the remaining ninety six milliseconds of that window the whole cgroup is not scheduled at all. Not slow, not preempted, not running.</p>

<p>Averaged over a minute, that is forty percent utilisation, which is exactly true and completely useless. The request that arrives at millisecond five of a window waits for the window to end before it does anything, and nothing in a utilisation graph has the resolution to show that.</p>

<p>The counter that shows it is the throttled seconds total, which we had never put on a dashboard. Those pods were being held for about sixty milliseconds of every hundred, hour after hour, for as long as the metric had existed.</p>

<p>Three things changed. The runtime now takes its parallelism from the cgroup limit rather than the node, so the work spreads across the period instead of burning it in a burst. Latency sensitive services kept their requests and lost their limits entirely, which was an uncomfortable conversation and the right outcome; batch work kept limits, because for batch a throttled period costs nothing. And every service dashboard carries a throttling panel next to CPU, with an alert when more than one period in twenty is capped.</p>

<p>Utilisation is an average taken over a second. Throttling happens inside a hundred milliseconds, and that is where the customer is waiting.</p>

<p>– Sergey Shinder</p>

      <guid>https://dev.to/intervixa_ai/devops-outage-scenario-solving-kubernetes-crashloopbackoff-probe-flapping-cold-starts-1ahi</guid>
      <description><p>In technical interviews for <strong>Senior Cloud, DevOps, and SRE roles</strong>, trivial syntax questions are gone. Hiring managers want to see how you respond when production is down at 2 AM.</p>

<p>Today, let's dissect a real-world production incident: <strong>Solving Kubernetes CrashLoopBackOff: Probe Flapping &amp; Cold Starts</strong>.</p>




<h2>
  
  
  The Scenario
</h2>

<blockquote>
<p><strong>Incident Context:</strong> A new container release enters CrashLoopBackOff because the DB connection pool takes 40s to warm up, but liveness probe kills it at 15s.</p>
</blockquote>

<p>When facing this situation during a live interview or outage, interviewers evaluate structured triage:</p>

<ol>
<li>Blast radius identification</li>
<li>Immediate traffic mitigation</li>
<li>Root cause isolation</li>
<li>Permanent architectural hardening</li>
</ol>




<h2>
  
  
  1. Immediate Incident Triage
</h2>

<p>Verify current telemetry and active states before applying code changes:<br>
</p>

<div class="highlight js-code-highlight">
<pre class="highlight shell"><code>kubectl describe pod &lt;pod-name&gt; <span class="nt">-n</span> prod | <span class="nb">grep</span> <span class="nt">-A</span> 5 <span class="s1">'Liveness:'</span>
kubectl logs &lt;pod-name&gt; <span class="nt">--previous</span>
kubectl get events <span class="nt">-n</span> prod <span class="nt">--sort-by</span><span class="o">=</span><span class="s1">'.metadata.creationTimestamp'</span>
</code></pre>

</div>






<h2>
  
  
  2. Root Cause Analysis (RCA)
</h2>

<p><strong>Why did this happen?</strong></p>

<p>Aggressive liveness probe timeouts before application initialization completes, creating an infinite restart loop.</p>




<h2>
  
  
  3. Permanent Architectural Hardening
</h2>

<p>Decouple readiness from liveness, and configure a dedicated startupProbe with failureThreshold=30 and periodSeconds=10.</p>

      <title>Designing for Assumed Compromise: Securing Autonomous AI Agents on Kubernetes</title>
      <dc:creator>Krishan Thisera</dc:creator>
      <pubDate>Fri, 18 Sep 2026 08:44:06 +0000</pubDate>
      <link>https://dev.to/krishanthisera/designing-for-assumed-compromise-securing-autonomous-ai-agents-on-kubernetes-38a2</link>
      <guid>https://dev.to/krishanthisera/designing-for-assumed-compromise-securing-autonomous-ai-agents-on-kubernetes-38a2</guid>
      <description><h3>
  
  
  A Defense-in-Depth Blueprint from Orchestration to Identity, Credentials, and Scale
</h3>

<p><strong>An agent sandbox</strong> is a runtime instance, a container, microVM, or Kubernetes pod, built to run an autonomous AI agent's generated code and tool calls behind an isolation boundary. That boundary is meant to keep a compromised session from reaching the host machine or other tenants. How effectively it does that depends on which isolation technique backs it. Autonomous coding and browsing agents built on large language models now routinely generate and execute code, install packages, browse the live web, and handle credentials. Each of those actions carries only probabilistic guarantees about what the model will do, and that uncertainty is the problem an agent sandbox exists to solve.</p>

<p>That combination compounds two risks: <strong>arbitrary code execution</strong> and instructions an attacker can influence through <strong>prompt injection</strong>. Together, they have pushed the infrastructure conversation away from asking whether a container is hardened enough, toward <strong>assuming the container will eventually be compromised</strong> and designing every layer around that assumption.</p>

<p><a href="https://media2.dev.to/dynamic/image/width=800%2Cheight=%2Cfit=scale-down%2Cgravity=auto%2Cformat=auto/https%3A%2F%2Fdev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com%2Fuploads%2Farticles%2Fwtdo1cp7abecqo6592n5.png" class="article-body-image-wrapper"><img src="https://media2.dev.to/dynamic/image/width=800%2Cheight=%2Cfit=scale-down%2Cgravity=auto%2Cformat=auto/https%3A%2F%2Fdev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com%2Fuploads%2Farticles%2Fwtdo1cp7abecqo6592n5.png" alt="Diagram of nested sandbox, runtime, network, identity and governance layers defending a Kubernetes-orchestrated agent against malicious code execution, prompt injection and data exfiltration" width="800" height="589"></a></p>

<p>This article covers that security posture, together with what it costs and how you govern a fleet of sessions rather than one, once you run it at scale.</p>

<h2>
  
  
  Chapter 1: The Kubernetes-Native Orchestration Primitive
</h2>

<p>Kubernetes offers two dominant workload abstractions. Deployments manage stateless, interchangeable pods, and StatefulSets manage numbered fleets with generic identities. Neither fits an agent session, a singleton needing a stable hostname, persistent storage, and a lifecycle that pauses and resumes rather than only starting and stopping. Teams hand-assembled a StatefulSet of one, a Service, and a persistent volume claim (PVC). That combination had no shared lifecycle controller.</p>

<p>The <strong>Sandbox</strong> custom resource definition (CRD), maintained by <a href="https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox" rel="noopener noreferrer"><code>kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox</code></a> under Kubernetes SIG Apps, closes that gap with a declarative API for one stateful pod with a stable identity. Three CRDs extend it:</p>

<ul>
<li>
<strong>SandboxTemplate</strong> enforces security defaults.</li>
<li>
<strong>SandboxWarmPool</strong> pre-provisions instances to cut cold-start latency.</li>
<li>
<strong>SandboxClaim</strong> lets a framework request an instance without managing the template.</li>
</ul>

<p><a href="https://media2.dev.to/dynamic/image/width=800%2Cheight=%2Cfit=scale-down%2Cgravity=auto%2Cformat=auto/https%3A%2F%2Fdev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com%2Fuploads%2Farticles%2Fikpa0ydh7sfbxmusvqxx.png" class="article-body-image-wrapper"><img src="https://media2.dev.to/dynamic/image/width=800%2Cheight=%2Cfit=scale-down%2Cgravity=auto%2Cformat=auto/https%3A%2F%2Fdev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com%2Fuploads%2Farticles%2Fikpa0ydh7sfbxmusvqxx.png" alt="Flow diagram from SandboxTemplate through SandboxWarmPool and SandboxClaim to an active Sandbox instance, with RuntimeClass providing delegated isolation" width="799" height="294"></a></p>

<h2>
  
  
  Chapter 2: Choosing an Isolation Technique
</h2>

<p>The Sandbox CRD manages a pod under the hood, so it inherits the standard Kubernetes <code>runtimeClassName</code> field for selecting the runtime, the same field any pod-based workload can set. <code>runc</code>, gVisor, and Kata Containers are the common runtime options it selects between, and seccomp layers a syscall filter on top of whichever one is chosen. Together the four trade isolation strength against cost differently. <code>runc</code> is the default low-level runtime that Docker and containerd use to create every container. It offers the least isolation of the four. It isolates a process using the host kernel's own namespaces and control groups (cgroups), so every container on a node shares a single kernel. That is fine for trusted code, but risky once an autonomous agent might run attacker-influenced instructions inside it.</p>

<p><a href="https://media2.dev.to/dynamic/image/width=800%2Cheight=%2Cfit=scale-down%2Cgravity=auto%2Cformat=auto/https%3A%2F%2Fdev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com%2Fuploads%2Farticles%2F2zbqc37syli2o43gavn5.png" class="article-body-image-wrapper"><img src="https://media2.dev.to/dynamic/image/width=800%2Cheight=%2Cfit=scale-down%2Cgravity=auto%2Cformat=auto/https%3A%2F%2Fdev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com%2Fuploads%2Farticles%2F2zbqc37syli2o43gavn5.png" alt="Diagram comparing the layers of full virtual machines, microVMs, containers and gVisor, from application to hardware" width="800" height="264"></a></p>

<p><strong>seccomp (secure computing mode)</strong> is a Linux kernel facility that lets an operator allowlist or denylist the syscalls a container may invoke, rejecting anything outside that list. It adds no new kernel boundary. The host kernel still handles every allowed syscall directly, which keeps it cheap enough to layer onto almost any container. According to NVIDIA, it is one item in a defense-in-depth stack, suited to trusted internal automation rather than genuinely untrusted, agent-generated code.</p>

<p><a href="https://gvisor.dev/" rel="noopener noreferrer">gVisor</a> adds the kernel boundary that seccomp does not. It interposes a user-space component called <strong>the Sentry</strong> between a container's processes and the real kernel. The Sentry intercepts every system call and handles it through a restricted reimplementation of the kernel surface. That shrinks the hundreds of syscalls a workload can reach down to a minimal, vetted subset. <strong>gVisor's overhead</strong> is commonly cited as <strong>10 to 30 percent</strong> on I/O-heavy workloads, with little impact on compute-heavy work such as model inference. According to gVisor's performance guide, though, overhead varies considerably by platform and workload, and small, syscall-heavy operations can exceed that range. That makes gVisor a strong fit for CPU-bound tasks and a weaker one for constant file or network I/O.</p>

<p><a href="https://katacontainers.io/" rel="noopener noreferrer">Kata Containers</a> provides the most isolation of the four, running a pod inside hardware-assisted virtualisation instead of a shared kernel. A hypervisor such as <a href="https://firecracker-microvm.github.io/" rel="noopener noreferrer">Firecracker</a> creates a genuinely separate virtual machine with its own guest kernel, using the processor's virtualisation features rather than the host kernel's namespaces. Firecracker is a purpose-built hypervisor developed at AWS to back Lambda and Fargate, with reported boot times clustering around <strong>100 to 125 milliseconds</strong> and memory overhead <strong>under 5 megabytes per microVM</strong>. Firecracker speaks its own API rather than Kubernetes', so Kata Containers closes that gap by implementing the standard <strong>Container Runtime Interface (CRI)</strong>. A Kata-backed pod then schedules through the same <code>kubectl apply</code> workflow, with only a <code>runtimeClassName</code> field marking the difference. Kata supports <a href="https://www.cloudhypervisor.org/" rel="noopener noreferrer">Cloud Hypervisor</a> as its default backend, with Firecracker and QEMU as alternatives, and boots in roughly <strong>150 to 300 milliseconds</strong>. Because the isolation boundary is an entire separate kernel, <strong>an attacker who compromises the workload still has to escape both the guest kernel and the hypervisor to reach the host</strong>. That closes off namespace abuse and kernel-level exploits regardless of what the agent inside does.</p>

<p><a href="https://media2.dev.to/dynamic/image/width=800%2Cheight=%2Cfit=scale-down%2Cgravity=auto%2Cformat=auto/https%3A%2F%2Fdev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com%2Fuploads%2Farticles%2F1eppb09p2ptvovt2gyqx.png" class="article-body-image-wrapper"><img src="https://media2.dev.to/dynamic/image/width=800%2Cheight=%2Cfit=scale-down%2Cgravity=auto%2Cformat=auto/https%3A%2F%2Fdev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com%2Fuploads%2Farticles%2F1eppb09p2ptvovt2gyqx.png" alt="Diagram of selecting a runtime via runtimeClassName — runc, gVisor or Kata Containers — with seccomp layered on top and each path's isolation boundary traced down to the host Kernel" width="800" height="582"></a></p>

<p>None of this comes free. Even at 100 to 300 milliseconds, microVM boot time is measurable overhead once multiplied across every agent turn in a busy pipeline. Running Kata in production also means managing nested virtualisation support and a larger per-pod memory footprint than a bare container carries. seccomp and gVisor trade some of that isolation strength back for lower cost and higher throughput, which is exactly why the <code>RuntimeClass</code> mechanism matters. A single cluster can run a short-lived code interpreter session under gVisor, tolerating little latency budget but running cheaply at high volume, alongside a long-running, browser-equipped agent under Kata or Firecracker, through the same API.</p>

<h3>
  
  
  Docker-in-Docker, isolated at the hypervisor level
</h3>

<p>Letting an agent build or run its own containers has conventionally meant <strong>Docker-in-Docker (DinD)</strong>, a nested daemon in privileged mode, or the host's Docker socket mounted directly into the container. Both are well-known escape vectors, acceptable for trusted CI/CD pipelines but not for an autonomous agent whose build steps could be influenced by a prompt injected through a compromised dependency.</p>

<p><a href="https://www.docker.com/products/docker-sandboxes/" rel="noopener noreferrer">Docker Sandboxes</a> removes both vectors instead of trying to harden them. Each agent runs inside its own rootless microVM with its own private Docker daemon, isolated at the hypervisor level rather than sharing the host's, with full privileges granted only inside that guest. In its "direct" mode, file changes still sync back to the host filesystem, so <strong>any git hooks, install scripts, or task configuration the agent touched need review before a human executes them locally.</strong> Closing this gap requires review discipline, not additional infrastructure. It means diffing hooks and checking scripts after each session.</p>

<h2>
  
  
  Chapter 3: Threat Modelling for Assumed Compromise
</h2>

<p>The central threat behind every isolation decision is <strong>indirect prompt injection</strong>. Direct prompt injection, a user typing malicious instructions into a chat box, is comparatively well understood. Indirect prompt injection hides those instructions inside content the agent is expected to read as normal work. Vectors include a compromised file in a repository, a pull request description, a configuration file such as <code>.cursorrules</code> or <code>CLAUDE.md</code>, and a response from an <a href="https://modelcontextprotocol.io/" rel="noopener noreferrer">MCP</a> (Model Context Protocol) server. According to NVIDIA's AI Red Team guidance on sandboxing agentic workflows, <strong>an agent cannot reliably tell an operator's instructions apart from text inside a document it was asked to process</strong>. That means anyone who can put content in front of it gains a channel for influencing its actions.</p>

<p>Filtering the prompt cannot close this gap. Agentic tools execute arbitrary code by design. Once an action passes into a subprocess, the application has no visibility into or control over what that subprocess does. A compromised agent can also route around an allowlist by calling a restricted tool indirectly through one that is already approved. According to NVIDIA's guidance, <strong>only isolation with a kernel boundary of its own can reliably contain the risk, because containment then does not depend on the model behaving as instructed</strong>.</p>

<p>NVIDIA's guidance replaces a binary trusted-or-not judgement with four escalating rules:</p>

<ul>
<li>
<strong>Non-overridable enterprise denylist.</strong> An absolute floor of blocked operations, such as reads or writes to credential files or hooks, that neither a user nor the agent can approve away.</li>
<li>
<strong>Workspace-scoped, allow-by-default access.</strong> Read and write permission inside the agent's active project directory, granted without approval for every action, since constant friction on routine work undermines the practice of approval altogether.</li>
<li>
<strong>Narrow allowlisted exceptions.</strong> Specific operations outside the workspace that the agent's job still requires, such as a named SSH key for a legitimate git operation, approved individually.</li>
<li>
<strong>Default-deny.</strong> Fresh manual approval required for everything else, never cached. A cached "yes" from an earlier legitimate action can be silently reused by an attacker-influenced action that looks similar later in the same session.</li>
</ul>

<p>The same principle underlies all four rules. Each applies <strong>least privilege continuously, rather than only once at startup</strong>. A kernel boundary limits what a compromised process can touch. A network allowlist limits where it can send data. A credential proxy, covered in Chapter 4, limits what it can ever possess. Each is the same idea, enforced at a different layer.</p>
