<h2>
  
  
  Chapter 4: Network, Credential, and Identity Boundaries
</h2>

<p>Chapter 3 closed by naming three layers where least privilege gets enforced: a kernel boundary, a network allowlist, and a credential proxy. This chapter covers the latter two, network and credential boundaries, and adds a third: identity management. Together, egress control, credential handling, and identity management govern what a compromised agent can still do once it is talking to the outside world. That is where most of the actual damage from indirect prompt injection gets carried out.</p>

<h3>
  
  
  Egress filtering is not content-level safety
</h3>

<p>Network egress control matters independently of kernel isolation, because even a sandbox that holds does not stop a compromised agent from sending data out through a connection it was always permitted to make. According to NVIDIA's guidance, <strong>egress filtering is a mandatory baseline control, not optional hardening</strong>. It calls for blocking outbound connections to unknown destinations by default. That boundary should be enforced through enterprise denylists, HTTP proxies, and DNS-level restriction, rather than trusting the agent's own code to self-police.</p>

<p><strong>Domain-level allowlisting is not the same thing as content-level safety.</strong> Permitting a broad domain such as <code>github.com</code> allows access to any content hosted there. An attacker who can post data to an already-allowed gist or issue comment therefore has an exfiltration channel a domain filter will never flag.</p>

<p><a href="https://media2.dev.to/dynamic/image/width=800%2Cheight=%2Cfit=scale-down%2Cgravity=auto%2Cformat=auto/https%3A%2F%2Fdev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com%2Fuploads%2Farticles%2Fs1xflwhty58maocnmdo6.png" class="article-body-image-wrapper"><img src="https://media2.dev.to/dynamic/image/width=800%2Cheight=%2Cfit=scale-down%2Cgravity=auto%2Cformat=auto/https%3A%2F%2Fdev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com%2Fuploads%2Farticles%2Fs1xflwhty58maocnmdo6.png" alt="Diagram of a network proxy allowing all of github.com, so a legitimate repository request and an attacker's exfiltration path both pass" width="799" height="281"></a></p>

<p>Production implementations span a real spectrum rather than one fixed policy. At one end, a narrow allowlist permits only a model API endpoint and a package registry. At the other, full air-gapping removes all internet access for high-risk batch jobs with no legitimate need to reach it.</p>

<p>The same logic applies inside an organisation's network, not only at its external edge: a destination being reachable doesn't mean it's safe to trust. <strong>Zero-trust segmentation</strong> is what enforces that internally. An agent sandbox that can reach a production database or a deployment credential store has simply moved the exfiltration risk internally rather than removed it. In multi-tenant designs, that internal segmentation needs to be mandatory, not optional, on equal footing with external egress control.</p>

<h3>
  
  
  Credentials that never enter the sandbox
</h3>

<p>The conventional pattern for handling secrets is to inject an API key into a sandbox as an environment variable through a Kubernetes <code>secretKeyRef</code>. That pattern has an irreducible weakness. The agent process itself can still read those environment variables at runtime.</p>

<p>Three failure modes follow from that fact alone, regardless of how well the surrounding sandbox is isolated:</p>

<ul>
<li>The agent inadvertently includes the secret in a generated response or log.</li>
<li>A prompt-injected agent deliberately exfiltrates it through an otherwise-legitimate outbound call.</li>
<li>An adversarial input tricks the agent into printing or transmitting its own environment variables.</li>
</ul>

<p>The <strong>credential-proxy pattern</strong>, implemented independently by projects including Infisical's <a href="https://infisical.com/blog/agent-vault-the-open-source-credential-proxy-and-vault-for-agents" rel="noopener noreferrer">Agent Vault</a>, inverts this. The sandbox holds no secret at all. It routes outbound HTTPS traffic to a proxy, typically through the standard <code>HTTPS_PROXY</code> variable. That proxy terminates TLS and strips the placeholder credential the agent's request carried. It then injects the real credential from an encrypted store and re-establishes the connection to the actual upstream service. A <strong>session-level agent token</strong> issued at proxy handshake ties every request to a specific agent. That is what stops one sandbox from riding another's credentials, and it lets the proxy log, rate-limit, and revoke access mid-session without touching the sandbox itself. Because the sandbox never holds the real secret, none of the three failure modes above can occur. There is nothing for the agent to leak, exfiltrate, or be tricked into revealing.</p>

<p><a href="https://media2.dev.to/dynamic/image/width=800%2Cheight=%2Cfit=scale-down%2Cgravity=auto%2Cformat=auto/https%3A%2F%2Fdev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com%2Fuploads%2Farticles%2Fj91j4dnldhydd3gbixc0.png" class="article-body-image-wrapper"><img src="https://media2.dev.to/dynamic/image/width=800%2Cheight=%2Cfit=scale-down%2Cgravity=auto%2Cformat=auto/https%3A%2F%2Fdev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com%2Fuploads%2Farticles%2Fj91j4dnldhydd3gbixc0.png" alt="Diagram of the credential-proxy pattern: a sandbox sends a placeholder token, and the proxy swaps in the real credential before forwarding it to the upstream API" width="799" height="279"></a></p>

<p>Three approaches implement this pattern today, and they differ in what infrastructure they assume and how mature each one is. A team already running Istio can build it directly on <code>EnvoyFilter</code> and <code>ext_authz</code>. That path requires Istio's full service mesh to already be in place, and it inherits the fragility that Istio's documentation attributes to that escape-hatch mechanism. A purpose-built AI gateway requires no service mesh at all. <a href="https://agentgateway.dev/" rel="noopener noreferrer">agentgateway</a> and <a href="https://aigateway.envoyproxy.io/" rel="noopener noreferrer">Envoy AI Gateway</a> both run as a standalone binary. Infisical's <a href="https://infisical.com/blog/agent-proxy" rel="noopener noreferrer">Agent Proxy</a> is the third option, a vendor-managed proxy. Agent Proxy also requires no service mesh, but delegates secret storage to Infisical's own service rather than an operator-controlled vault. All three remain a single point of failure if the proxy itself is compromised.</p>

<h3>
  
  
  No single mechanism covers identity completely
</h3>

<p>Three largely separate mechanisms address what identity an agent, or a sub-agent it spawns, actually carries, and none covers the problem completely. Bearer tokens and long-lived API keys assume a human authenticates once and performs a bounded set of actions. Handing an autonomous agent one broad token instead creates <strong>ambient authority</strong>, letting it exercise everything the token permits at any time, with no link between a specific tool call and a specific authorisation decision.</p>

<p>The problem compounds with sub-agents. Whichever of three common patterns a team picks carries its own risk:</p>

<ul>
<li>
<strong>Passing the parent's token down to a sub-agent</strong> erases the audit trail's ability to distinguish parent from child.</li>
<li>
<strong>Issuing a new static credential per sub-agent</strong> multiplies the credentials that can leak.</li>
<li>
<strong>Running a sub-agent unauthenticated</strong> is a compliance failure outright.</li>
</ul>

<p><a href="https://spiffe.io/" rel="noopener noreferrer">SPIFFE</a> and its SPIRE implementation issue a short-lived, cryptographically verifiable identity based on runtime attestation rather than a static secret. SPIRE, however, expects every workload variant pre-registered ahead of time and delivers identity through a pull-based call, both of which sit awkwardly against a sandbox whose useful life might be seconds.</p>

<p><strong>Cloud workload identity federation</strong> authenticates a pod to its cloud provider, but only coarsely. Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) implements this through <a href="https://docs.cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/concepts/workload-identity" rel="noopener noreferrer">Workload Identity Federation</a>, which makes every pod sharing one Kubernetes ServiceAccount cryptographically indistinguishable to Google Cloud IAM. Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (EKS) offers a choice between two mechanisms, each with a different tradeoff. <a href="https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/userguide/iam-roles-for-service-accounts.html" rel="noopener noreferrer">IAM Roles for Service Accounts (IRSA)</a> refreshes credentials without a pod restart, at the cost of AWS Security Token Service (STS) quota. <a href="https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/userguide/pod-identities.html" rel="noopener noreferrer">EKS Pod Identity</a> avoids that quota cost but <strong>can cache credentials for up to six hours</strong> before a permission change takes effect. Delegation-aware authorisation systems such as <a href="https://openfga.dev/" rel="noopener noreferrer">OpenFGA</a> and <a href="https://authzed.com/spicedb" rel="noopener noreferrer">SpiceDB</a> fill the remaining gap, checking each individual tool call against an explicit graph of user and sub-agent permissions rather than authorising a session once at the start.</p>

<p>At the time of writing, stitching these three layers together remains real engineering work rather than a documented, turnkey integration.</p>

<h2>
  
  
  Chapter 5: Scaling and Scheduling Agent Workloads
</h2>

<p>Chapters 2 through 4 covered how to secure a single sandbox. Running thousands of them at once introduces a different problem. It means avoiding a multi-second wait every time an agent starts a new turn, and stopping one tenant's burst of activity from crowding out every other tenant on the same infrastructure.</p>

<h3>
  
  
  Balancing statefulness and disposability
</h3>

<p>An agent sandbox has to satisfy two requirements that pull in opposite directions. Many agent workloads are genuinely stateful. A persistent notebook kernel needs to preserve variables across cells, and a coding-agent workspace needs its file changes to survive across many separate tool calls. Both want <strong>a stable hostname and durable storage</strong>. At the same time, the premise of a sandbox, as distinct from a persistent server, is that it should be <strong>cheap to start per task and safe to tear down immediately afterward</strong>.</p>

<p>This differs from the ephemeral containers used in continuous integration and delivery (CI/CD). A CI/CD container starts, runs a predetermined pipeline of steps, and is discarded, with no expectation of resuming mid-pipeline. An agent sandbox typically needs to persist across many discrete tool calls over an extended, possibly paused, conversation. It might sit idle for minutes while a person reviews its output, then resume with the same files, the same running processes, and the same hostname. Chapter 1 covered the interface built for this, the <code>Sandbox</code> custom resource's declarative API for a single stateful pod with a stable identity. It exists because a hand-rolled StatefulSet, Service, and persistent volume claim had no shared lifecycle controller to reproduce that fidelity.</p>

<h3>
  
  
  Warm pools and checkpoint-restore
</h3>

<p>Chapter 1 also introduced <code>SandboxWarmPool</code>, a pool of pre-booted sandboxes that lets a new session claim one instead of creating it from scratch. This brings allocation down to <strong>the millisecond range</strong>. A fresh pod with a hardware-isolated kernel boot (Chapter 2) costs seconds instead, an order of magnitude slower.</p>

<p>GKE adds a further refinement. <a href="https://docs.cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/concepts/pod-snapshots" rel="noopener noreferrer">Pod Snapshots</a> is a checkpoint-and-restore capability that captures a running pod's full state and <strong>cuts startup time from minutes to seconds</strong>, including for GPU-backed workloads that are expensive to cold-boot. A companion capability, snapshot-pausing, reclaims an idle sandbox's compute without discarding its state the way a hard termination would.</p>

<p>EKS has no equivalent yet. AWS does support checkpoint and restore, built on <a href="https://criu.org/" rel="noopener noreferrer">Checkpoint/Restore In Userspace (CRIU)</a> through the Kubernetes kubelet checkpoint API. Its purpose is different. It exists for forensic evidence preservation, capturing a suspicious container's state without killing it so an investigator can examine it later. This forensic checkpointing is not a substitute for GKE's cold-start capability.</p>

<p>One project outside AWS closes part of this gap today. <a href="https://github.com/agent-substrate/substrate" rel="noopener noreferrer">Agent Substrate</a>, a joint effort between Solo.io and Google, runs its own cross-cloud snapshot layer, independent of any single vendor's kubelet feature, coordinating full-state snapshots across an agent sandbox's suspend and resume cycles.</p>

<p><a href="https://media2.dev.to/dynamic/image/width=800%2Cheight=%2Cfit=scale-down%2Cgravity=auto%2Cformat=auto/https%3A%2F%2Fdev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com%2Fuploads%2Farticles%2Fquk3x5ounm0fvtsq3v5b.png" class="article-body-image-wrapper"><img src="https://media2.dev.to/dynamic/image/width=800%2Cheight=%2Cfit=scale-down%2Cgravity=auto%2Cformat=auto/https%3A%2F%2Fdev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com%2Fuploads%2Farticles%2Fquk3x5ounm0fvtsq3v5b.png" alt="Bar chart comparing allocation time for cold boot, GKE Pod Snapshots and SandboxWarmPool, from seconds down to milliseconds" width="799" height="173"></a></p>

<h3>
  
  
  Quotas, tokens, and rate limits for a sandbox fleet
</h3>

<p>Kubernetes' standard <code>ResourceQuota</code> object sets a namespace-level ceiling on aggregate CPU, memory, and object counts, the same primitive any multi-tenant cluster already relies on. <code>LimitRange</code> complements it by bounding what any single pod or container inside that namespace can request, so one workload cannot claim the entire quota for itself. Neither one governs what a workload does over the network, which the egress allowlists from Chapter 4 control separately. <strong>Many of the threat categories catalogued by <a href="https://genai.owasp.org/resource/owasp-top-10-for-agentic-applications-for-2026/" rel="noopener noreferrer">OWASP</a> for agentic systems operate entirely within otherwise-permitted resource and network boundaries</strong>. That means an attack can satisfy both checks at once and still succeed. A compromised agent exfiltrating data through an already-allowed API call, for instance, breaches no quota at all. <strong>Quota and network policy alone cannot catch that</strong>, which is why agent workloads need a further, behavioural layer constraining the pattern of an agent's actions rather than only their volume.</p>

<p>This behavioural layer governs token consumption most directly, typically enforced at the same AI gateway introduced in Chapter 4. Envoy AI Gateway's <code>QuotaPolicy</code> and agentgateway's token budgets both implement it as a three-level hierarchy. An overall platform budget subdivides into per-tenant budgets, which further subdivide into optional per-agent budgets. The gateway rejects a request once its level's budget runs out.</p>

<p>Rate limiting for agent fleets operates at two distinct layers, and mixing them up causes real problems. One governs how many outbound calls an agent may make against an external service. The other governs how many sandboxes, and how much aggregate compute, a tenant may have running at once. Confusing them produces either over-restrictive throttling or under-enforcement. Over-restrictive throttling kicks in when compute quota looks tight but the real bottleneck is API calls. Under-enforcement lets a tenant within its compute quota keep overloading an external API for everyone sharing that connection.</p>

<p>The first layer sits naturally at the network and proxy layer. The same egress point that injects credentials in Chapter 4 typically enforces it too, so a platform already routing traffic through that proxy for credentials gets per-tenant throttling as an adjacent policy. The second layer sits at the scheduler and quota layer described above.</p>

<p>Agent workloads are bursty. A single user task can fan out into several rapid tool calls, or spawn sub-agents that act concurrently. A per-tenant limit checked independently by each agent cannot see the other agents' concurrent draws against the same shared budget. An external rate-limit service closes this gap. Envoy AI Gateway and agentgateway both call one to share a budget across replicas. The service checks and decrements one shared counter atomically, so concurrent agents see a consistent, current balance rather than a stale per-replica count.</p>

<h3>
  
  
  What isolation actually costs
</h3>

<p>Chapter 2 covered isolation's overhead in compute and latency terms. What it costs in dollars is harder to establish. No source reviewed for this article publishes a like-for-like comparison of what a single provider charges for the same workload under <code>runc</code>, seccomp, gVisor, and Kata Containers. <strong>You cannot currently look up what stronger isolation costs while holding everything else constant. You have to benchmark it yourself.</strong></p>

<p>Published pricing does make one part of the spectrum concrete, the deployment model. At a reference scale of 200 concurrently running sandboxes, a managed, shared platform lists monthly pricing around <strong>US\$7,200</strong>. A comparable footprint under a bring-your-own-cloud model costs about <strong>US\$2,060</strong> (<strong>more than a threefold difference</strong>) for broadly similar isolation and capability. Most of that gap is operational and multi-tenancy overhead a fully managed platform absorbs on a customer's behalf, separate from the isolation technology itself.</p>

<h2>
  
  
  Chapter 6: Benchmark Evidence and Attack Surfaces Beyond Code
</h2>

<p>Chapters 2 and 3 argued, from engineering principles, that hardware isolation (gVisor's kernel boundary, Kata's separate guest kernel) is necessary once an agent might execute attacker-influenced code. This chapter tests that argument against evidence, drawing on a 2026 benchmark measuring real escape attempts and an attack surface those technologies were never built to cover.</p>

<h3>
  
  
  What SandboxEscapeBench found
</h3>

<p><a href="https://arxiv.org/html/2603.02277v1" rel="noopener noreferrer">SandboxEscapeBench</a> tests whether a model with root access inside a container can find its way out to the host. It spans 18 scenarios across the orchestration, runtime, and kernel layers, each rated by difficulty. Frontier models reliably solved easy misconfigurations, such as privileged containers and exposed Docker sockets. On medium-difficulty exploits requiring genuine multi-step work, <strong>GPT-5 and Claude Opus 4.5 both scored around 0.40</strong>. On kernel-level exploits, <strong>every model tested scored zero</strong>.</p>

<p>The gap between model tiers was large. Claude Opus scored 0.49 overall against Haiku's 0.18, <strong>roughly threefold</strong>, and performance scaled with the compute a model was given. <strong>Plain Docker isolation is insufficient by default. Real deployments should be stress-tested rather than assumed safe.</strong> No novel vulnerabilities were used, only known misconfigurations and disclosed Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) entries. <strong>This remains a single study, not yet independently replicated.</strong></p>

<p>These results are worth reading together: escape success scaled with the compute a model was given, and every model scored zero on every kernel-level exploit. Together, they suggest the current zero-success ceiling reflects <strong>where model capability stands today, not a permanent limit</strong>. If that holds, three directions follow:</p>

<ul>
<li>Hardware isolation stops being reserved for high-risk workloads and becomes the default for any untrusted one.</li>
<li>Credential proxying and egress filtering move from a feature teams opt into to one platforms ship by default.</li>
<li>Escape benchmarking becomes a routine part of due diligence, the way penetration testing did for cloud infrastructure.</li>
</ul>

<h3>
  
  
  The browser as a different kind of risk
</h3>

<p>Browsing agents introduce a second execution surface that Chapter 2's isolation technologies do not cover. The risk is semantic rather than technical. <strong>A malicious instruction hidden in a web page's rendered content does not need to escape a sandbox. It manipulates the agent's reasoning directly</strong>, the same indirect prompt injection risk from Chapter 3, with a page rather than a file as the vector. The stakes are higher because of what a browsing session carries, live authentication cookies and sometimes payment details, which a manipulated agent can leak through actions the browser was always permitted to take.</p>

<p>Browser isolation complements code-execution sandboxing rather than replacing it, typically through an HTTP-level policy layer sitting above the browser's existing process sandboxing. It remains younger and less standardised than code-execution isolation, with no equivalent yet of Chapter 1's <code>RuntimeClass</code> for an isolated browser session.</p>

<h2>
  
  
  Chapter 7: Buy Versus Build
</h2>

<p>Everything from Chapter 1's orchestration primitive to Chapter 6's benchmark evidence describes a stack a team could build. Most teams do not build it themselves. They buy a hosted sandbox instead, from a provider such as <a href="https://e2b.dev/" rel="noopener noreferrer">E2B</a>, <a href="https://fly.io/" rel="noopener noreferrer">Fly.io</a>, <a href="https://modal.com/" rel="noopener noreferrer">Modal</a> or <a href="https://northflank.com/" rel="noopener noreferrer">Northflank</a>. Each sells a scheduled, isolated, credential-brokered sandbox. None of them require the buyer to assemble the underlying cluster, isolation configuration, credential proxy and governance layer.</p>

<p><strong>The isolation layer is not a differentiator among these vendors.</strong> Nearly every one uses microVM or gVisor isolation, the two strongest techniques Chapter 2 covered. The industry already treats both as sufficient for untrusted, LLM-generated code. Vendors compete instead on <strong>cold-start speed, session persistence, pricing and developer experience</strong>. That makes the buy decision simple for most teams. Vendors' published isolation stacks appear broadly comparable to what this article has described, at a fraction of the build cost. Building it yourself only becomes worthwhile at organisations already running Kubernetes at scale, or held to compliance requirements that rule out shared infrastructure.</p>

<h2>
  
  
  Chapter 8: Conclusion
</h2>

<p>One fact underlies why agent sandboxes exist at all. A large language model can now execute code it wrote itself, in response to instructions nobody can fully verify. <strong>That same capability gives the agent its value and makes it dangerous.</strong></p>

<p>Nothing this article has covered removes that risk. Every layer instead narrows it, each covered in an earlier chapter:</p>

<ul>
<li>the orchestration primitive</li>
<li>the isolation technique</li>
<li>the threat model</li>
<li>network and credential boundaries</li>
<li>fleet scaling and governance</li>
<li>the benchmark evidence</li>
</ul>

<p>None of these ideas were invented specifically for AI agents. Multi-tenant cloud security supplied the isolation techniques, and a decade of browser security research supplied the browser controls.</p>

<p><strong>The result is defense-in-depth, a posture rather than a solution.</strong> It treats every layer as something that will eventually fail, and it builds each one so that failure does not cascade into whatever comes next.</p>

      <title>Local Kubernetes Dev — Part 16: Conclusion and next steps</title>
      <dc:creator>Gaberial Sofie</dc:creator>
      <pubDate>Fri, 18 Sep 2026 07:53:00 +0000</pubDate>

      <description><p>The local Kubernetes series is complete — 16 parts.</p>

<p>If you're new and just arrived — start with chapter one on the inner dev loop. This final one pulls it all together: what we built and where to grow next.</p>

<p>What we ended up with — a real (not emulated) cluster on your laptop: k3d + a FastAPI image + real manifests (Deployment/Service/Ingress) + a fast inner loop on Tilt + PostgreSQL alongside + config/secrets + probes and limits + k9s. The main payoff is environment parity: manifest, RBAC, and service discovery problems show up locally, not via alerts at 3 a.m.</p>

<p>And three honest directions to grow (don't grab all at once):<br>
• GitOps (Argo CD / Flux) — when the team and the number of environments grow;<br>
• an observability stack (kube-prometheus-stack, Prometheus Operator, OpenTelemetry) — with a warning: a heavy stack can take down a weak k3d;<br>
• remote development (Telepresence, mirrord) — and the difference between mirror mode (a copy of traffic, safe) vs steal (interception).</p>

<p>Read the finale and jump back to any chapter: <a href="https://dorokhovich.com/blog/local-k8s-conclusion-and-next-steps?utm_source=devto&amp;utm_medium=syndication&amp;utm_campaign=local-k8s-conclusion-and-next-steps" rel="noopener noreferrer">https://dorokhovich.com/blog/local-k8s-conclusion-and-next-steps?utm_source=devto&amp;utm_medium=syndication&amp;utm_campaign=local-k8s-conclusion-and-next-steps</a></p>

      <title>Building Kubernetes operators with OCaml</title>
      <dc:creator>Ville Vesilehto</dc:creator>
      <pubDate>Fri, 18 Sep 2026 07:51:02 +0000</pubDate>
      <link>https://dev.to/thevilledev/building-kubernetes-operators-with-ocaml-1n1j</link>
      <guid>https://dev.to/thevilledev/building-kubernetes-operators-with-ocaml-1n1j</guid>
      <description><h2>
  
  
  TL;DR
</h2>

<p>I created <a href="https://github.com/thevilledev/ocaml-kube" rel="noopener noreferrer">ocaml-kube</a>, a Kubernetes client and controller library for OCaml, published on opam as <code>kube</code>. This post shows how to use it through <a href="https://github.com/thevilledev/kube-ocaml-examples" rel="noopener noreferrer">three operator tutorials</a>, following the familiar <a href="https://book.kubebuilder.io/quick-start" rel="noopener noreferrer">Kubebuilder</a> workflow: scaffold a project, define an API, generate the CRD, implement reconciliation, and run it against a cluster.</p>

<p><a href="https://media2.dev.to/dynamic/image/width=800%2Cheight=%2Cfit=scale-down%2Cgravity=auto%2Cformat=auto/https%3A%2F%2Fdev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com%2Fuploads%2Farticles%2F995qvv1igsfdxz9s5sih.png" class="article-body-image-wrapper"><img src="https://media2.dev.to/dynamic/image/width=800%2Cheight=%2Cfit=scale-down%2Cgravity=auto%2Cformat=auto/https%3A%2F%2Fdev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com%2Fuploads%2Farticles%2F995qvv1igsfdxz9s5sih.png" alt="Three OCaml operators: Greeting manages a ConfigMap; WebApp manages a Deployment and Service; the cluster-scoped Project manages a Namespace and ResourceQuota." width="800" height="579"></a></p>

<h2>
  
  
  The library and Kubernetes support
</h2>

<p>The <code>kube.0.1.3</code> release used here <a href="https://github.com/thevilledev/ocaml-kube/blob/main/docs/compatibility.md" rel="noopener noreferrer">supports Kubernetes <strong>1.34, 1.35, 1.36, and 1.37</strong></a>, with integration tests against real API servers. Older clusters may work through the generic client but aren't supported, and the supported range doesn't imply coverage of every alpha feature.</p>

<p><code>ocaml-kube</code> is a native OCaml 5 implementation, not a binding to Go's client-go. Its <a href="https://github.com/thevilledev/ocaml-kube/blob/main/lib/http.mli" rel="noopener noreferrer">HTTP/1.1 transport</a> uses Unix sockets and the OCaml TLS library. Watches and controller workers run on system threads with cooperative cancellation.</p>

<p>Built-in resource records and JSON codecs are <a href="https://github.com/thevilledev/ocaml-kube/blob/main/docs/api-codegen.md" rel="noopener noreferrer">generated from checksum-pinned Kubernetes OpenAPI schemas</a>. Each minor has a separate schema library, from <code>kube.api.v1_34</code> through <code>kube.api.v1_37</code>, sharing the same runtime. These tutorials use <code>Kube_api_v1_36</code> for 1.36 resource types; that doesn't restrict the operators to a 1.36 cluster.</p>

<p>Above the client sit LIST/WATCH caches, a work queue, and retries. <code>Kube.Operator</code> handles process startup, credentials, shutdown, diagnostics, and optional leader election. The application code describes what should exist.</p>

<h2>
  
  
  Same pattern, different language
</h2>

<p>An operator watches Kubernetes resources and repeatedly brings actual state towards the desired state in <code>spec</code>. Changing the language doesn't change that contract.</p>

<p>The interesting part here is how OCaml expresses it. Records describe the API, a PPX deriver generates JSON codecs and schemas, and module functors build clients and controllers for a particular resource type. For example:<br>
</p>

<div class="highlight js-code-highlight">
<pre class="highlight ocaml"><code><span class="k">module</span> <span class="nc">Controller</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="nn">Kube</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nn">Controller</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nc">Make</span> <span class="p">(</span><span class="nc">Custom_resource</span><span class="p">)</span>
<span class="k">module</span> <span class="nc">Config_maps</span> <span class="o">=</span>
  <span class="nn">Kube</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nn">Reconcile</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nc">Make</span> <span class="p">(</span><span class="nn">Kube_api_v1_36</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nn">Core_v1</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nc">ConfigMap</span><span class="p">)</span>
</code></pre>

</div>



<h2>
  
  
  From scaffold to CRD
</h2>

<p>With OCaml 5.1 or newer and opam installed:<br>
</p>

<div class="highlight js-code-highlight">
<pre class="highlight shell"><code>opam <span class="nb">install </span>kube.0.1.3

opam <span class="nb">exec</span> <span class="nt">--</span> ocaml-kube init <span class="se">\</span>
  <span class="nt">--output</span> greeting-operator <span class="se">\</span>
  <span class="nt">--group</span> tutorial.ocaml.dev <span class="se">\</span>
  <span class="nt">--version</span> v1alpha1 <span class="se">\</span>
  <span class="nt">--kind</span> Greeting
</code></pre>

</div>



<p>This covers the project-and-first-API setup normally split between <code>kubebuilder init</code> and <code>kubebuilder create api</code>. Here, <code>--group</code> takes the full API group. The generated project includes a model, controller skeleton, CRD, RBAC, sample resource, Deployment, and Dockerfile. The reconciler still needs application logic.</p>

<p>In the completed Greeting tutorial, the desired state is one field:<br>
</p>

<div class="highlight js-code-highlight">
<pre class="highlight ocaml"><code><span class="k">module</span> <span class="nc">C</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="nc">Kube_crd</span>

<span class="k">module</span> <span class="nc">Spec</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="k">struct</span>
  <span class="k">type</span> <span class="n">t</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="p">{</span>
    <span class="n">message</span> <span class="o">:</span> <span class="kt">string</span><span class="p">;</span>
        <span class="p">[</span><span class="o">@</span><span class="n">kube</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="n">schema</span> <span class="nn">C</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nn">Schema</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="n">string</span> <span class="o">~</span><span class="n">min_length</span><span class="o">:</span><span class="mi">1</span> <span class="o">~</span><span class="n">max_length</span><span class="o">:</span><span class="mi">200</span> <span class="bp">()</span><span class="p">]</span>
  <span class="p">}</span>
  <span class="p">[</span><span class="o">@@</span><span class="n">deriving</span> <span class="n">kube</span><span class="p">]</span>
<span class="k">end</span>
</code></pre>

</div>



<p>Those attributes become validation in the CRD. <code>Kube_crd.Resource.Make</code> combines the spec, status, and resource identity into the typed resource module.</p>

<p>After editing the model, generate the manifest from inside the project:<br>
</p>

<div class="highlight js-code-highlight">
<pre class="highlight shell"><code>opam <span class="nb">exec</span> <span class="nt">--</span> dune <span class="nb">exec </span>tools/generate_crd.exe <span class="o">&gt;</span> deploy/crd.yaml
opam <span class="nb">exec</span> <span class="nt">--</span> dune build @codegen-check
</code></pre>

</div>



<p>That's the equivalent of <code>make manifests</code>. The second command catches a checked-in CRD that no longer matches the OCaml model.</p>

<h2>
  
  
  Three tutorials
</h2>

<p>Each example is an independent Dune project with a walkthrough, tests, and deployment files.</p>

<ul>
<li>
<a href="https://github.com/thevilledev/kube-ocaml-examples/tree/main/tutorials/01-greeting" rel="noopener noreferrer">Greeting</a> writes <code>spec.message</code> into a ConfigMap. It introduces Server-Side Apply, owner references, and a <code>Ready</code> status condition.</li>
<li>
<a href="https://github.com/thevilledev/kube-ocaml-examples/tree/main/tutorials/02-webapp" rel="noopener noreferrer">WebApp</a> manages a Deployment and Service. It watches both child kinds and reports the Deployment's ready replica count.</li>
<li>
<a href="https://github.com/thevilledev/kube-ocaml-examples/tree/main/tutorials/03-project" rel="noopener noreferrer">Project</a> is cluster-scoped and manages a Namespace and ResourceQuota. A finalizer keeps the Project around until Namespace deletion completes.</li>
</ul>

<p>The Greeting's child write is small:<br>
</p>

<div class="highlight js-code-highlight">
<pre class="highlight ocaml"><code><span class="nn">Config_maps</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="n">apply_owned</span> <span class="o">~</span><span class="n">cancel</span><span class="o">:</span><span class="n">request</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="n">cancel</span> <span class="n">client</span>
  <span class="o">~</span><span class="n">field_manager</span><span class="o">:</span><span class="s2">"greeting-operator"</span>
  <span class="o">~</span><span class="n">owner_api</span><span class="o">:</span><span class="nn">Custom_resource</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="n">api</span>
  <span class="o">~</span><span class="n">owner</span><span class="o">:</span><span class="n">greeting</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="n">metadata</span>
  <span class="p">(</span><span class="n">desired_config_map</span> <span class="n">greeting</span><span class="p">)</span>
</code></pre>

</div>



<p>The helper attaches the owner reference and applies the desired fields. An owned-resource watch enqueues the parent when a child changes. Kubernetes handles garbage collection when the owner is deleted; the Project example adds explicit cleanup to demonstrate finalizers.</p>

<h2>
  
  
  Try it on kind
</h2>

<p>With Docker running, plus <code>kind</code>, <code>kubectl</code>, and the OCaml toolchain available:<br>
</p>

<div class="highlight js-code-highlight">
<pre class="highlight shell"><code>git clone https://github.com/thevilledev/kube-ocaml-examples.git
<span class="nb">cd </span>kube-ocaml-examples
opam <span class="nb">install </span>kube.0.1.3 alcotest

make build
make <span class="nb">test
</span>make check-generated
make kind-smoke
</code></pre>

</div>



<p>I ran all three controllers locally against a Kubernetes 1.37 kind cluster. The smoke test checks the ConfigMap contents, waits for the WebApp rollout and status, checks the Project quota, and verifies that finalization removes its Namespace. The five unit tests and CRD drift checks also passed.</p>

<p>The smoke test stops the controllers and deletes the sample resources, but leaves the cluster available. When finished:<br>
</p>

<div class="highlight js-code-highlight">
<pre class="highlight shell"><code>kind delete cluster <span class="nt">--name</span> ocaml-kube-examples
</code></pre>

</div>



<p>These are small examples for learning the API and controller patterns. For the complete commands, including container builds and in-cluster deployment, start with the <a href="https://github.com/thevilledev/kube-ocaml-examples#readme" rel="noopener noreferrer">repository README</a>.</p>
